title: Political Legitimacy and Authority
subtitle: Why should anyone obey the state, and what if no one has to?
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish power, legitimacy, authority and political obligation
By the end you will be able to explain Weber's three types of legitimate rule and his definition of the state
By the end you will be able to reconstruct and criticise the consent, fair play and service theories of authority
By the end you will be able to state Robert Paul Wolff's argument for philosophical anarchism and the main replies to it
hook:
It is 3 a.m. You are at a red light in an empty town. There is no traffic, no camera, no police car, and you can see clearly for half a mile in every direction. Most people still wait. Why?

Perhaps habit. Perhaps fear of a hidden camera. But many people would say something stranger: that the law simply *tells* them to wait, and that this matters in itself. Notice how odd that is. A command from a stranger with a gun is just a threat. A command from the state seems to many of us to be something more: a reason. This lesson asks what could possibly turn force into authority, and whether it ever really does. It is one of the oldest questions in politics. Socrates faced it in his cell (Day 10), Hobbes built a Leviathan to answer it (Day 42), and Locke and Rousseau gave rival solutions (Days 52–53). Now we will look at it with the sharper tools of modern political philosophy.

sections.heading: Four Words That Are Easy to Confuse
sections.body:
Political philosophers use four related terms, and much confusion comes from blurring them.

**Power** is the ability to make people do things, whether they want to or not. A mafia boss has power. So does an occupying army.

**Legitimacy** is the property that makes the exercise of power *rightful*. A legitimate state is one that is morally permitted to make and enforce laws. Some philosophers think legitimacy is only this permission, a kind of moral licence to coerce.

**Authority** is stronger. To have authority over you is to have the right to *command* you in a way that gives you a reason to obey just because you were commanded. Think of the difference between a friend who gives good advice and a referee who blows a whistle. You follow the friend's advice because it is good; you stop playing when the referee whistles because the referee said so.

**Political obligation** is the flip side of authority: a moral duty, binding on citizens, to obey the laws of their own state, because they are its laws. If political obligation exists, you have a reason to wait at the red light even when waiting achieves nothing.

One more distinction matters. Sociologists talk about **descriptive legitimacy**: whether people in fact *believe* their rulers are rightful. Philosophers mostly care about **normative legitimacy**: whether the rulers really *are* rightful. A regime can be believed legitimate and not be (a popular dictatorship), or be legitimate and not believed so. Keep these apart and many arguments become clearer.

sections.heading: Weber: The Monopoly of Force and Three Kinds of Legitimacy
sections.body:
The German sociologist **Max Weber** (1864–1920) gave the most famous modern definition of the state in a 1919 lecture, *Politics as a Vocation*, delivered in Munich amid the chaos following Germany's defeat in the First World War. The state, he said, is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

Every word earns its place. *Monopoly*: others (parents, private guards) may use force only because the state permits it. *Claims*: the state says its force is rightful; whether it is, is another question. *Territory*: the state's claim is tied to a piece of land.

Weber then asked, as a sociologist, why people actually accept rule. He found three pure types of legitimate authority:

1. **Traditional authority**: obedience because things have always been so. A hereditary king rules because his ancestors did.
2. **Charismatic authority**: obedience to a person seen as extraordinary, a prophet, war hero or revolutionary leader. It is powerful but unstable; it tends to collapse or become routine when the leader dies.
3. **Legal-rational authority**: obedience to impersonal rules, enacted by correct procedures, applied by officials who hold an office rather than own it. A tax inspector has authority because of her position in a rule-governed bureaucracy, not because of who she is.

Weber's types are *descriptive*. They tell us what people believe makes power rightful, not whether they are correct. A legal-rational regime can pass monstrous laws by perfectly proper procedures. So the philosopher's question remains: which, if any, of these grounds actually creates a duty to obey?

sections.heading: Consent and Its Troubles
sections.body:
The most natural answer is **consent**. Promises create obligations: if I agree to feed your cat, I now owe it to you. So if citizens agreed to obey the state, they would be bound. This is the heart of the social contract tradition you met with Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.

The obvious problem is that almost no one has actually agreed. Naturalised citizens take an oath, but most people are simply born into a state. Locke (Day 52) saw this and appealed to **tacit consent**: by enjoying the protection of the laws, owning property, even travelling freely on the highway, you silently agree to the state's authority.

David Hume, whom you met on Days 49–50, mocked this in his essay *Of the Original Contract* (1748). He compared the poor peasant who knows no foreign language and lives on small wages to a man carried aboard a ship while asleep, who is told he has consented to the captain's command because he has not leapt into the ocean. Consent only counts if refusing it is a real option. For most people, emigration is costly, dangerous, or legally impossible, and wherever they go, they meet another state making the same demands.

A second move is **hypothetical consent**: the state is legitimate if rational people *would* agree to it, as in Rawls's original position (Day 82). But critics answer, as Ronald Dworkin put it in a 1973 essay on Rawls, that a hypothetical contract is not a weaker version of a real contract; it is no contract at all. That I *would* have agreed to sell you my car for a fair price does not mean you may take it. Hypothetical consent may show that a state is just, but it seems not to show that I have *bound myself* to it.

sections.heading: Fair Play, Natural Duties and Raz's Service Conception
sections.body:
If consent fails, other foundations have been proposed.

**Fair play.** H. L. A. Hart (1955) and the young John Rawls (1964) argued that when people restrict their liberty to run a cooperative scheme that benefits everyone, those who benefit owe it to the others to do their share. Free-riding on a fair scheme is unfair. Since the state is a vast cooperative scheme (roads, defence, public health), citizens owe their share: obedience.

Robert Nozick replied with a famous example in *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* (1974). Your neighbours set up a public address system and assign each household one day a year to run it with music and news. You enjoy listening from your window. When your day arrives, must you spend it at the microphone? Most people say no: benefits you did not ask for, and could not refuse, do not obligate you. Defenders reply that the state provides benefits like security that everyone needs, unlike a neighbourhood radio. The debate is unresolved.

**Natural duty.** The mature Rawls switched to a different idea: we all have a *natural duty of justice*, owed to everyone regardless of consent, to support just institutions that apply to us. The difficulty is **particularity**: if my duty is to support justice in general, why do I owe special obedience to *my* state rather than to whichever state is most just?

**The service conception.** Joseph Raz (*The Morality of Freedom*, 1986) offered a subtler test. His **normal justification thesis** says an authority is legitimate over you when you would better conform to the reasons that already apply to you by following its directives than by trying to work things out yourself. Traffic law is the perfect case. You already have reason to drive safely and to coordinate with others, but you cannot negotiate with every driver. Following a single rule, drive on the left, say, does better than acting on your own judgment. On Raz's view authority is *piecemeal*: a state might have authority over you on traffic or food safety, where its expertise and coordinating role exceed yours, but not on matters where you know better.

sections.heading: Wolff's Challenge: Philosophical Anarchism
sections.body:
In 1970 the American philosopher Robert Paul Wolff published a short, sharp book, *In Defense of Anarchism*. Its argument is easy to state and hard to escape.

1. Every person has a primary duty of **autonomy**: to take responsibility for their own actions by deciding for themselves what they ought to do. This is a Kantian idea (recall Kant's ideal of self-legislation from Day 56).
2. To accept authority is to do something *because you were commanded*, not because you judged it right.
3. So accepting authority means giving up autonomy.
4. Therefore, there can be no legitimate state that claims authority over autonomous persons.

Wolff considered one escape: **unanimous direct democracy**, where every law is one each person has personally voted for. Then obeying the law is just obeying yourself. But unanimity is impossible in any real society, and majority rule means the minority obeys laws it rejected.

Notice what Wolff did *not* say. He did not say we should throw bombs or that every law should be broken. The law against murder still binds you, but because murder is wrong, not because the law forbids it. This view is called **philosophical anarchism**: the claim that no existing state has genuine authority, combined with the recognition that we may still have excellent reasons to comply with many of its laws. It differs from *political anarchism*, which actively seeks to abolish the state.

A. John Simmons (in *Moral Principles and Political Obligations*, 1979, and later work) developed a more modest version. Having examined consent, fair play, gratitude and natural duty, he concluded that none grounds a *general* obligation for most citizens to obey. But he distinguished **justification** from **legitimacy**: a state may be morally justified, good to have around, better than the alternatives, without having the specific right to command *you*.

sections.heading: Replies and What Is at Stake
sections.body:
Critics of Wolff press several points.

First, his notion of autonomy may be too demanding. We constantly and reasonably defer to others: patients follow doctors, hikers follow guides. Raz would say that following a genuine authority is not abandoning your judgment but *exercising* it: you judge that you will do better by deferring. Deferring is itself an autonomous decision, just as Ulysses autonomously had himself tied to the mast.

Second, some argue that coordination problems give the state a special role that no individual can fill. If everyone acted on their own judgment about which side of the road to drive on, about property boundaries, or about punishments, the result would be chaos, what Hobbes called the war of all against all. On this view authority is not a threat to autonomy but a precondition for a world in which autonomous plans can succeed.

Third, **democratic** theorists argue that when people disagree reasonably, the fair way to settle the matter is an equal say for all. Thomas Christiano and Jeremy Waldron hold that respecting a democratic decision you voted against is a way of treating your fellow citizens as equals. Refusing to defer amounts to claiming your judgment counts for more than theirs.

Why does this matter beyond seminar rooms? Because the answer shapes how we think about **civil disobedience**, tax resistance, conscientious objection and revolution. If there is a strong general obligation to obey, breaking the law needs a heavy justification. If philosophical anarchism is right, the question in each case is simply whether the act is right, and the law's say-so adds little or nothing. Most philosophers today sit somewhere between: legitimacy comes in degrees, depends on how just and democratic a state is, and may cover some domains better than others. Socrates, refusing to escape his cell in the *Crito*, took the strong view. Many readers since have wondered whether he was right.

keyQuote.text: A state is a human community that (successfully) claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
keyQuote.source: Max Weber, Politics as a Vocation (1919), trans. Gerth and Mills

modernConnection.title: Why People Actually Obey: Procedural Justice and Platform Courts
modernConnection.body:
Philosophers ask whether we *ought* to obey; social scientists ask why we *do*. In *Why People Obey the Law* (1990), the psychologist Tom Tyler surveyed Chicago residents about their encounters with police and courts. A striking finding: people's willingness to comply depended less on whether they got a favourable outcome, or feared punishment, than on whether they felt they had been treated fairly: listened to, treated with respect, judged by neutral rules. This research on **procedural justice** has since shaped police training programmes in several countries.

This is Weber's descriptive legitimacy in action, and it carries a warning. A state that loses perceived legitimacy must rely more on force, which is expensive and tends to deepen distrust. Declining trust in governments, recorded in many countries by long-running surveys, is therefore not a soft cultural problem but a structural one.

The same question now arises outside the state. Large online platforms make rules for billions of people: what you can post, who gets banned. In 2020 Meta launched an Oversight Board, a body of outside experts that can overturn some of its content decisions. Whatever you think of it, it is an explicit attempt to borrow legitimacy from legal-rational forms: published rules, reasoned decisions, an appeals process.

The comparison is illuminating but imperfect. Platforms do not hold a monopoly of physical force, and you can (in theory) leave. Hume's peasant on the ship is relevant again, though: when all your friends, customers and news live on one platform, how real is the option to jump overboard? The philosophical lesson is that procedures can earn belief, but only substantive justice and real voice can earn rightful authority.

vocabulary.definition: The moral right of a state or institution to exercise power, especially to make and enforce rules.
vocabulary.example: Critics argued that a government installed by a coup lacked legitimacy, however stable it appeared.

vocabulary.definition: The right to command, such that a directive gives the subject a reason to comply simply because it was issued.
vocabulary.example: The referee's authority means the players stop when the whistle blows, even if they think the foul was imaginary.

vocabulary.definition: A moral duty of citizens to obey the laws of their own state because they are its laws.
vocabulary.example: If there is political obligation, you have a reason to wait at a red light on an empty road.

vocabulary.definition: Locke's idea that people silently agree to a government's authority by living under it and enjoying its benefits.
vocabulary.example: Hume doubted that tacit consent counts when leaving the country is not a realistic option.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that those who benefit from a fair cooperative scheme owe it to the other participants to do their share.
vocabulary.example: On the principle of fair play, someone who enjoys public roads and defence must pay taxes and obey the law.

vocabulary.definition: Raz's claim that an authority is legitimate when following its directives helps you conform better to reasons that already apply to you.
vocabulary.example: Food safety rules pass the normal justification thesis because regulators know more about bacteria than most cooks.

vocabulary.definition: The view that no existing state has genuine authority or creates a general duty to obey, without urging the state's violent abolition.
vocabulary.example: A philosophical anarchist still refuses to steal, but because stealing is wrong, not because the law forbids it.

vocabulary.definition: Whether people in fact believe a regime has the right to rule, as opposed to whether it really does.
vocabulary.example: Opinion polls measure descriptive legitimacy, not whether the government deserves trust.

thinkingExercise.title: The Red Light Test
thinkingExercise.prompt: Take three laws you obey: one minor (a traffic or parking rule), one about money (taxes), and one serious (a law against assault). For each, ask whether the law itself gives you a reason to comply, or whether you would do the same thing without it.
steps: For each law, write down your honest main reason for obeying: fear, habit, agreement with its purpose, respect for the process that made it, or something else.
Apply Raz's test: would you do better at what you already have reason to do by following the law than by using your own judgment? Where does the test give a clear yes, and where not?
Now play Wolff's advocate: is there any case where you obey *only* because the law says so? Does that feel like a loss of autonomy or a reasonable deferral?
Finally, describe one situation in which you think breaking one of these laws would be justified. What does your answer reveal about how strong you think political obligation is?

summary: Power, legitimacy, authority and political obligation are distinct; the hardest question is whether states have authority that creates a duty to obey.
Weber defined the state by its claimed monopoly of legitimate force and described traditional, charismatic and legal-rational legitimacy, but his account is descriptive.
Actual and tacit consent face Hume's objection that most people cannot realistically refuse; hypothetical consent may show justice but not self-binding.
Fair play, natural duty and Raz's service conception each ground some obligations, but face problems of unchosen benefits, particularity and piecemeal scope.
Wolff argued that authority and autonomy are incompatible; philosophical anarchists like Simmons separate a state's justification from its legitimacy.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between legitimacy and authority, as many philosophers use the terms?
options: Legitimacy is about history, authority about law
Legitimacy is a permission to coerce; authority adds a right to be obeyed because one commanded
Authority applies only to democracies, legitimacy to all states
There is no difference; the words are synonyms
quiz.explanation: A state could be permitted to enforce rules (legitimacy) without its commands giving you a content-independent reason to obey (authority).

quiz.question: Which of Weber's types best describes a tax official whose power comes from her office in a rule-governed bureaucracy?
options: Traditional authority
Charismatic authority
Legal-rational authority
Hypothetical authority
quiz.explanation: Legal-rational authority attaches to offices defined by impersonal rules, not to persons or ancestral custom.

quiz.question: Weber's three types of legitimacy tell us which regimes really deserve obedience.
quiz.explanation: Weber's account is descriptive: it explains why people believe in rulers' legitimacy, not whether that belief is correct.

quiz.question: Hume's image of a man carried aboard a ship while asleep is aimed at which idea?
options: Tacit consent
The principle of fair play
Charismatic authority
The natural duty of justice
quiz.explanation: Hume argues that staying put does not signify consent when leaving is practically impossible, undermining Locke's tacit consent.

quiz.question: Nozick's public address system example is meant to show that:
options: Democracy requires unanimity
Receiving benefits you did not seek or could not refuse does not by itself obligate you
States must provide entertainment to be legitimate
Hypothetical consent is binding
quiz.explanation: The example targets the fair play principle: enjoying an imposed benefit seems not to create a duty to contribute.

quiz.question: According to Raz's normal justification thesis, when is an authority legitimate over you?
options: When you have explicitly promised to obey it
When most citizens believe it is legitimate
When following its directives helps you conform better to reasons that already apply to you
When it has the strongest army in the territory
quiz.explanation: Raz's service conception grounds authority in its ability to help you act on your own reasons better than you could alone.

quiz.question: Wolff's philosophical anarchism implies that people should break laws whenever they can get away with it.
quiz.explanation: Wolff holds that laws lack authority, not that their content is wrong; there may be excellent independent reasons to act as many laws require.

quiz.question: The 'particularity problem' for natural duty theories asks:
options: Why I owe special obedience to my own state rather than to just institutions in general
Whether particular laws can be unjust
How a particular person can consent
Whether charisma can be routinised
quiz.explanation: A general duty to support justice does not obviously single out my own state as the one I must obey.

quiz.question: Tom Tyler's research suggests people comply with law mainly when:
options: Punishments are severe
They win their cases
They feel they were treated fairly by neutral procedures
They have formally consented
quiz.explanation: Tyler found perceived procedural fairness was a stronger driver of compliance than outcomes or fear of sanctions.

quiz.question: Simmons distinguishes a state's being morally justified from its having legitimate authority over a particular person.
quiz.explanation: For Simmons a state can be good and worth supporting without having the special right to command you.

goDeeper.body:
A lively recent debate concerns whether democracy itself is the source of authority. Defenders of the **instrumental** view (like Raz, or the epistocrats you will meet in Lesson 3) think authority depends on producing good results: a regime is legitimate to the extent that obeying it makes outcomes better. Defenders of the **intrinsic** or proceduralist view think democracy has value in itself because it is the only way of making collective decisions that treats each person as an equal when people reasonably disagree. Jeremy Waldron's *Law and Disagreement* (1999) argues that because we disagree about justice itself, we cannot make legitimacy depend on getting justice right; we need a fair procedure for deciding, and majority rule among equals is that procedure.

Another frontier is the legitimacy of institutions beyond the state: the European Union, the World Trade Organization, the International Criminal Court. Allen Buchanan and Robert Keohane proposed that global institutions can be legitimate without democratic consent if they meet standards like minimal moral acceptability, comparative benefit and institutional integrity, together with transparency that lets outsiders hold them to account. Critics worry that this lowers the bar. Finally, David Estlund's *Democratic Authority* (2008) tries to combine both camps: democracy has authority because it is a procedure that tends to get things right, and which no reasonable citizen could object to, a position he calls epistemic proceduralism.

readings.title: In Defense of Anarchism
readings.author: Robert Paul Wolff
readings.note: Short and punchy; the first chapter states the conflict between autonomy and authority.

readings.title: Politics as a Vocation
readings.author: Max Weber
readings.note: The 1919 lecture: read the opening pages on the state and legitimacy, and the closing pages on the ethics of responsibility.

readings.title: Moral Principles and Political Obligations
readings.author: A. John Simmons
readings.note: The classic systematic review of consent, fair play, gratitude and natural duty.

readings.title: Of the Original Contract
readings.author: David Hume
readings.note: A brief, witty essay containing the ship argument against tacit consent.

questions: Can a state be legitimate for some of its citizens but not for others, for instance for those who have no realistic way to leave?
If you think Wolff is wrong, where exactly does his argument fail: in his idea of autonomy, or in his claim that accepting authority means giving it up?
Should online platforms aim for legitimacy in the political sense, or is that a category mistake?
